subtopic_detail: IM adrenaline banded dose in anaphylaxis
stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to your regional emergency department after biting into a peanut butter biscuit at a birthday party 25 minutes ago. Within minutes he developed lip swelling, an urticarial rash across his trunk and a hoarse cry. He was given a friend's EpiPen Jr on scene and improved briefly, then his breathing worsened again in the ambulance.

On arrival he has a widespread urticarial rash, audible inspiratory stridor at rest and mild wheeze on auscultation. He is alert and clinging to his mother. His weight in the ambulance was documented as 15 kg. There is no personal history of asthma; he was previously known only to have a mild egg allergy. His father carries a family EpiPen for shellfish allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Urticarial rash, lip swelling, inspiratory stridor at rest, mild expiratory wheeze, no cyanosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intramuscular adrenaline dose?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed
options.rationale: ASCIA banded dosing gives 150 micrograms (EpiPen Jr equivalent) for children weighing 10 to 20 kg; per-kilogram arithmetic is not the Australian standard. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed
options.rationale: 300 micrograms is the ASCIA band for children 20 kg and above; a 15 kg child sits in the 10 to 20 kg band and receives 150 micrograms. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms per kilogram of 1:1000 into the deltoid, repeat every 5 minutes as needed
options.rationale: Per-kilogram arithmetic is discouraged by ASCIA for AU practice because banded dosing is faster and less error-prone in a crisis. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 75 micrograms into the anterolateral thigh, repeat every 3 minutes as needed
options.rationale: 75 micrograms is the ASCIA band for infants under 10 kg; a 15 kg child receives 150 micrograms and 3-minute cycling is not the standard interval. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 1 microgram per kilogram infusion started before any further intramuscular dose is given
options.rationale: IV adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after repeated IM doses and only in a monitored setting; IM remains the first-line route. (Source: ASCIA Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis in a child is treated with intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh, dosed by a banded age/weight table published by ASCIA. The three bands are under 10 kg (75 micrograms), 10 to 20 kg (150 micrograms) and over 20 kg (300 micrograms). Doses are repeated every 5 minutes if there is no improvement. IV adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory cases in a monitored setting. Second-line therapies (fluids, oxygen, salbutamol for wheeze) do not replace timely IM adrenaline. Documentation of the trigger and a discharge action plan with an EpiPen prescription are mandatory.
key_points: ASCIA bands: <10 kg 75 mcg, 10-20 kg 150 mcg, >20 kg 300 mcg.
IM anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes as needed.
Per-kg arithmetic is not the Australian standard.
IV infusion is second-line after repeated IM doses fail.
explanation.pearls: For a 15 kg child in anaphylaxis, give IM adrenaline 150 micrograms (ASCIA 10 to 20 kg band) into the anterolateral thigh and repeat every 5 minutes; avoid per-kg arithmetic in the crisis.

stem:
A 5-week-old exclusively breastfed boy is brought to your emergency department by his mother with a 6-hour history of poor feeding and one episode of blood-tinged vomit. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated home birth attended by a private midwife. His mother declined all injections after birth for her son, including vitamin K, on personal grounds. He has otherwise been well until this morning.

On examination he is pale and irritable but rousable. His anterior fontanelle is full and tense. There is bruising over the left flank without a history of trauma. His mucous membranes are pale and dry. There is no rash. Point-of-care venous glucose is 3.8 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5). His mother has no personal or family bleeding disorder history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 174/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 50/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, irritable but rousable, tense anterior fontanelle, unexplained left flank bruise, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 74 g/L (105-135); platelets 260 x10^9/L (150-450); INR 5.8 (0.9-1.2); APTT 82 seconds (25-38); fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (1.5-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Give a single dose of oral vitamin K 2 mg with plans for repeat oral doses at 1 week and 6 weeks
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K is inadequate for active bleeding; parenteral vitamin K plus a fresh frozen plasma transfusion is required to correct the coagulopathy rapidly. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding

options.text: Administer intravenous vitamin K 1 mg and transfuse fresh frozen plasma 10 to 20 mL per kilogram immediately
options.rationale: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding with intracranial signs and an INR above 5 needs IV vitamin K plus fresh frozen plasma to restore clotting rapidly while workup proceeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding

options.text: Give intravenous four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units per kilogram as sole therapy for the coagulopathy
options.rationale: PCC alone does not correct the underlying vitamin K deficiency; vitamin K is essential to restore ongoing factor synthesis. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding

options.text: Transfuse cryoprecipitate 5 mL per kilogram to correct suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation before further tests
options.rationale: Fibrinogen is normal and DIC is unlikely; cryoprecipitate will not correct the vitamin K-dependent factor deficit driving the coagulopathy. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding

options.text: Arrange non-contrast head computed tomography before any coagulation product to characterise the bleed first
options.rationale: Correcting life-threatening coagulopathy takes priority; imaging can proceed once vitamin K and FFP are running and vital signs stabilise. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding

explanation.summary: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurs between 2 weeks and 6 months in exclusively breastfed infants who did not receive parenteral vitamin K at birth. Presentation is often intracranial with sudden collapse, bulging fontanelle and unexplained bruising. Laboratory features are a markedly prolonged INR and APTT with normal fibrinogen and platelets. Treatment is immediate IV vitamin K 1 mg plus fresh frozen plasma 10 to 20 mL/kg. Head imaging follows resuscitation. Prevention is a single IM dose of vitamin K 1 mg at birth (or a three-dose oral schedule if parents refuse IM), and Australian practice strongly recommends the IM route because oral courses are frequently missed.
key_points: Late VKDB presents 2 weeks to 6 months in unsupplemented breastfed infants.
INR and APTT are prolonged with normal fibrinogen and platelets.
Treatment is IV vitamin K plus fresh frozen plasma.
IM vitamin K at birth is the AU standard for prevention.
explanation.pearls: In late VKDB with intracranial signs, give IV vitamin K 1 mg plus fresh frozen plasma 10 to 20 mL/kg immediately; imaging follows resuscitation.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding
NHMRC Vitamin K Prophylaxis for Newborns

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia oral iron dosing
stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to your general practice for a routine check by her mother. She drinks about 900 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle and eats limited solids. She has been pale for months but is otherwise well, meeting motor milestones and gaining weight along the 25th centile. There is no history of bleeding, prior surgery, or chronic diarrhoea, and she has never been transfused.

On examination she is pale but alert and playful. There is no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. Her heart sounds are dual with a soft flow murmur that disappears on standing. She has slightly spoon-shaped nails but no glossitis. Recent bloods show haemoglobin 82 g/L (110-140), MCV 66 fL (75-87), ferritin 6 microgram/L (12-150), and a normal reticulocyte count. Coeliac serology is negative and she has no blood in her stools.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, playful, soft flow murmur that resolves on standing, mild koilonychia, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 82 g/L (110-140); MCV 66 fL (75-87); ferritin 6 mcg/L (12-150); reticulocytes normal; coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management plan?

options.text: Reduce cow's milk to no more than 500 mL daily and start oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg per kilogram elemental iron once daily
options.rationale: Milk restriction is correct but AU dosing is 3 to 6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron and once-daily dosing without dietary counselling misses the drivers of the deficiency. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Refer for intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion because oral iron is unlikely to correct a haemoglobin below 90 g/L
options.rationale: Uncomplicated iron deficiency in a toddler with adequate oral intake responds to oral iron; IV iron is reserved for oral intolerance or malabsorption. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Reduce cow's milk to no more than 500 mL daily, start oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg per kilogram elemental iron daily and recheck the FBC in 4 to 6 weeks
options.rationale: AU paediatric practice is to limit cow's milk to under 500 mL/day (an oral iron chelator and calorie displacer), give 3 to 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron and reassess response at 4 to 6 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Recommend dietary iron enrichment alone and repeat the full blood count in 3 months without pharmacological iron replacement
options.rationale: Symptomatic microcytic anaemia with a ferritin below 12 will not correct on dietary changes alone within a reasonable timeframe. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Transfuse packed red blood cells 10 mL per kilogram now to raise the haemoglobin above 90 g/L before dietary changes
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or very severe anaemia; a well child with a flow murmur alone does not need blood. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency in Australian toddlers is most often driven by high cow's milk intake, which displaces iron-rich solids and chelates iron in the gut. The clinical picture is a pale but well child with a low haemoglobin, low MCV and low ferritin; a flow murmur is common at this depth of anaemia. First-line management is to reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL/day, encourage iron-rich solids, and start oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron. Response is monitored by repeat FBC at 4 to 6 weeks; continue treatment for a further 3 months after normal haemoglobin to replenish stores. IV iron is reserved for oral intolerance or malabsorption; transfusion for haemodynamic compromise only.
key_points: Cow's milk above 500 mL/day is the dominant driver in Australian toddlers.
Oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron is first-line.
Recheck FBC at 4 to 6 weeks; treat for 3 months after normalisation.
IV iron for intolerance or malabsorption; transfusion for haemodynamic compromise.
explanation.pearls: In a 2-year-old with iron deficiency and high cow's milk intake, cap milk at 500 mL/day, start oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg/kg elemental iron daily, and recheck the FBC at 4 to 6 weeks.

stem:
A 6-week-old term boy is brought to your metropolitan emergency department after a single episode in his cot 90 minutes ago. His mother heard a choking noise, found him limp and cyanotic around the mouth, gently repositioned him and he pinked up and cried within 20 to 30 seconds. He has fed normally since and slept in her arms in the waiting room. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, is exclusively breastfed and is on no medications. There has been no coryza, no fever and no vomiting.

On examination he is alert, feeding vigorously and interactive. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no bruising, no rash and no dysmorphism. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable. Point-of-care venous glucose is 4.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5). His growth is on the 50th centile and his mother has no smoking history. No family member has died suddenly in infancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 90/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, feeding well, no bruising, no dysmorphism, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care glucose 4.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); ECG within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management plan?

options.text: Admit for a minimum 24-hour period of continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and inpatient metabolic screen
options.rationale: His age under 60 days meets one high-risk criterion, but admission with routine cardiorespiratory monitoring alone is not required if he is well after a period of observation; investigation is targeted, not comprehensive. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Send home immediately with red-flag advice and a follow-up appointment with his general practitioner in a week
options.rationale: His age under 60 days places him outside the low-risk criteria; some observation and targeted testing are required before discharge. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Perform full septic workup with lumbar puncture, empirical intravenous antibiotics and admission for 48 hours of observation
options.rationale: Full septic workup is not indicated in a well, afebrile infant with a single BRUE; targeted testing is preferred. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Observe with continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours, obtain pertussis PCR and ECG, and involve senior paediatrics before disposition
options.rationale: His age below 60 days classifies him as higher risk; the AAP recommendation is targeted observation, pertussis testing (Australian pertussis burden), an ECG to exclude long QT, and senior involvement before discharge. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Arrange a home apnoea monitor before discharge and refer for outpatient echocardiography within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Home apnoea monitors do not reduce sudden infant death and are not recommended after an isolated BRUE. (Source: AAP BRUE Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: A brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) is a sudden brief episode of cyanosis or pallor, altered breathing, altered tone or altered responsiveness in an infant under 12 months that has fully resolved and has no medical explanation after history and examination. Low-risk criteria are age over 60 days, gestation at least 32 weeks and at least 45 weeks post-conceptual age, first BRUE, duration under 60 seconds, no CPR by a trained provider and no concerning history or examination findings. Low-risk infants can be discharged after brief observation. Higher-risk infants need targeted testing (typically ECG for long QT, pertussis PCR in Australia, a period of monitored observation and specialist involvement) rather than a shotgun workup. Home apnoea monitors are not recommended.
key_points: Low-risk BRUE requires age above 60 days plus other criteria.
Higher-risk infants get targeted testing, not a shotgun workup.
ECG for long QT and pertussis PCR are AU-relevant tests.
Home apnoea monitors do not reduce sudden infant death.
explanation.pearls: In an infant under 60 days after BRUE, use targeted observation with ECG and pertussis PCR rather than a shotgun workup; home apnoea monitors are not recommended.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

stem:
A 7-month-old boy is brought to your regional emergency department by his mother with 8 hours of intermittent crying episodes lasting minutes at a time, during which he draws his legs up and appears very distressed. Between episodes he has been lethargic and floppy on his mother's shoulder. He had two episodes of non-bilious vomiting and one soft stool that his mother describes as looking like dark red jam.

On examination he is pale and quiet between episodes with cool peripheries and capillary refill of three seconds. Abdomen is soft with a long thin lump palpable in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are increased. Rectal examination reveals dark red mucus on the examining finger. He is otherwise well grown and fully immunised. A point-of-care ultrasound in the department shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant. He is haemodynamically stable after a single 20 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min post fluid, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes, long thin right upper quadrant mass, dark red mucus per rectum, increased bowel sounds, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant; venous blood gas within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue observation for another 4 hours with intravenous maintenance fluids alone because reduction may occur spontaneously
options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception rarely reduces spontaneously and delay increases the risk of bowel necrosis and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Prescribe oral ondansetron 2 mg with plain film abdominal radiography before considering any intervention today
options.rationale: Plain film has poor sensitivity for intussusception when ultrasound is already diagnostic, and antiemetic alone will not treat the mechanical obstruction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Refer to general paediatrics for outpatient contrast enema imaging in the next few days after initial rehydration
options.rationale: Intussusception is a paediatric emergency requiring same-shift reduction; deferring beyond hours risks bowel loss. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Prepare for emergency laparotomy with primary bowel resection because ultrasound-confirmed intussusception is a surgical diagnosis
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for failed enema, peritonism or evidence of perforation; first-line is image-guided pneumatic (air) reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Arrange urgent radiology-led pneumatic (air) enema reduction under paediatric surgical cover once resuscitation is adequate
options.rationale: After adequate resuscitation, image-guided pneumatic reduction is first-line for uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception in Australia, with surgery on standby for failure or perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception typically presents between 3 months and 3 years with episodic colicky pain, lethargy between episodes, vomiting and dark blood-and-mucus stool that families often describe as jam-like. A right upper quadrant mass is classically described. Ultrasound has replaced plain film as the imaging of choice and shows a target sign in cross-section. After resuscitation, image-guided pneumatic (air) reduction under paediatric surgical cover is first-line in Australia, with success rates around 80 to 90 percent. Surgery is reserved for enema failure, peritonism, perforation or the identification of a pathological lead point. Recurrence after successful reduction is 5 to 10 percent, typically within 24 hours.
key_points: Ultrasound target sign confirms diagnosis; plain film is unnecessary.
Pneumatic (air) enema is first-line reduction after resuscitation.
Surgery for enema failure, peritonism, perforation or lead point.
Recurrence rate is 5 to 10 percent, mostly within 24 hours.
explanation.pearls: After resuscitation of a child with ultrasound-confirmed intussusception, arrange radiology-led pneumatic (air) enema reduction under paediatric surgical cover, not primary laparotomy.

stem:
A previously well 3-year-old boy is brought to your rural emergency department by ambulance with a 12-hour illness of high fever, leg pain and vomiting. In the last 2 hours he has become increasingly floppy and pale and his mother has noticed several purple spots on his ankles that do not blanch. Retrieval to the tertiary paediatric centre has been requested and is estimated at 90 minutes.

On arrival he is grunting, mottled, with cold peripheries and capillary refill of 5 seconds. There is a non-blanching purpuric rash spreading on his lower limbs and abdomen with two large lesions greater than 2 cm across. Neck is soft and Brudzinski is negative. His weight is 15 kg. Point-of-care blood glucose is 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0). Intraosseous access has been obtained after failed IV attempts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 96 percent on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 39.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, non-blanching purpuric rash with two lesions greater than 2 cm, grunting respirations
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.22, lactate 4.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); coagulation and FBC pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antibiotic and dose to administer via the intraosseous line now?

options.text: Intraosseous ceftriaxone 100 mg per kilogram (maximum 4 g) as a single dose, given after a 20 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus
options.rationale: AU paediatric sepsis pathway with meningococcaemia features gives IV/IO ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) empirically after initial fluid bolus. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal Disease)

options.text: Intraosseous benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kilogram (maximum 3 g) as a single dose, then re-evaluate before further antibiotics
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin can be given if third-generation cephalosporins are unavailable, but empirical ceftriaxone gives broader early cover in the AU protocol. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal Disease)

options.text: Intraosseous amoxicillin 50 mg per kilogram plus gentamicin 7 mg per kilogram as first-line antimicrobial regimen
options.rationale: This is a neonatal septic regimen; a 3-year-old with suspected meningococcaemia receives ceftriaxone empirically. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal Disease)

options.text: Intraosseous vancomycin 15 mg per kilogram as monotherapy before any other antibiotic is started
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy does not cover Neisseria meningitidis; a third-generation cephalosporin is empirically required. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal Disease)

options.text: Intraosseous cefotaxime 25 mg per kilogram as a single reduced dose because he is already in septic shock
options.rationale: Cefotaxime is an acceptable alternative to ceftriaxone but the empirical dose is 50 mg/kg 6-hourly (not reduced); reducing the dose in shock is not correct. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningococcal Disease)

explanation.summary: Meningococcal septicaemia presents with fever, non-blanching rash, limb pain, poor circulation and rapid deterioration. Empirical antibiotic must not wait for cultures or a lumbar puncture. The AU standard for the paediatric septic pathway is IV or IO ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (maximum 4 g) after obtaining blood cultures where possible, plus early aggressive fluid resuscitation (20 mL/kg saline boluses to 60 mL/kg total) and early involvement of the paediatric retrieval service. Adjuncts include dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for suspected bacterial meningitis (pre or with first antibiotic dose), close monitoring for adrenal insufficiency and DIC, and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts once the diagnosis is confirmed.
key_points: IV/IO ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) empirically for suspected meningococcaemia.
Aggressive fluid resuscitation to 60 mL/kg with reassessment for pulmonary oedema.
Do not delay antibiotic for lumbar puncture in unstable patient.
Contact chemoprophylaxis follows confirmation of diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: In paediatric meningococcaemia, give IO ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) after the first saline bolus; do not delay antibiotic for lumbar puncture in the unstable child.

stem:
A 12-day-old boy is brought to your regional emergency department by his parents with 2 days of poor feeding, vomiting and increasing sleepiness. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, discharged at day 3 after normal newborn screening bloodspots. He is exclusively breastfed with occasional formula top-ups. His parents describe him as normal until day 10.

On examination he is pale, floppy and mottled with poor tone. His anterior fontanelle is soft and mucous membranes are dry. Genitals appear normal male with descended testes and no obvious virilisation. His weight today is 3.0 kg, down from 3.4 kg at birth. Bedside investigations reveal sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5), venous pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-30) and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). No infection focus is identified after examination and initial cultures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Floppy, mottled, dry mucous membranes, normal male genitalia with descended testes, no ambiguity
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 6.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); venous glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-30); lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Empirical intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg per kilogram and admit for full septic workup and observation over 24 hours
options.rationale: Sepsis is a differential but the sodium, potassium and glucose picture in a normal-appearing male neonate with weight loss points to salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia; antibiotics alone will not save this child. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg immediately, 10 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus with 10 percent dextrose, and correction of hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: The electrolyte and glucose profile in an unwell male neonate with weight loss is classic for salt-losing CAH; stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, saline and dextrose are life-saving. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 0.1 mg as an initial single dose with intravenous normal saline maintenance over 24 hours
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no IV formulation and works slowly; hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity in acute crisis. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Intravenous insulin 0.05 units per kilogram per hour with 10 percent dextrose to lower the serum potassium before further therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose alone does not correct the underlying adrenal insufficiency and risks hypoglycaemia in a hypoglycaemic neonate; hydrocortisone is the priority intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 3 mL per kilogram as first-line correction of the severe hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Rapid correction with hypertonic saline is dangerous in salt-losing CAH; isotonic saline with hydrocortisone corrects the sodium safely as the cortisol deficit resolves. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most commonly 21-hydroxylase deficiency) presents around day 7 to 14 of life with weight loss, poor feeding, vomiting, dehydration and shock. The biochemical hallmark is hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis and hypoglycaemia. Males have no genital ambiguity to prompt earlier diagnosis, so shock may be the presenting feature; newborn bloodspot screening for 17-hydroxyprogesterone helps but a false-negative is possible. Emergency treatment is IV hydrocortisone (25 mg for infants, 50 mg for children under 5 years) which provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, plus normal saline bolus and dextrose. Long-term management is oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone with stress dosing during illness.
key_points: Presents day 7 to 14 with weight loss, shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia.
Males lack genital ambiguity, so recognition depends on biochemistry.
Emergency treatment is IV hydrocortisone plus saline and dextrose.
Rapid correction of sodium with hypertonic saline is dangerous.
explanation.pearls: In a well-appearing male neonate collapsing at day 7 to 14 with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, give IV hydrocortisone 25 mg with saline and dextrose without waiting for the ACTH stimulation test.

sources.label: APEG Consensus Guidelines for Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizure with disconfirming metabolic finding
stem:
A term 36-hour-old girl is reviewed by you on the postnatal ward after nursing staff observed a 90-second episode of rhythmic left-sided facial twitching with bicycling limb movements. She was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean for breech presentation. Her mother has no medical history; there was no maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes or perinatal hypoxia (Apgars 9 and 9). Her mother is breastfeeding, with normal feed volumes so far.

On examination between episodes she is pink, alert and moving all four limbs symmetrically. Anterior fontanelle is soft. There is no rash. Head circumference is on the 50th centile. Point-of-care venous glucose is 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-5.5). Serum sodium is 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), venous ammonia 42 micromol/L (<50). Cerebrospinal fluid is bland with normal glucose and no organisms. A cranial ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 68/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive between episodes, symmetrical limb movement, soft fontanelle, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145); calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.60); magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.7-1.0); ammonia 42 mcmol/L (<50); CSF bland; cranial ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous phenobarbitone 20 mg per kilogram loading dose without further metabolic testing today
options.rationale: Empirical phenobarbitone is standard for confirmed neonatal seizures but does not answer the diagnostic question; targeted metabolic workup should proceed in parallel. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures)

options.text: Request an urgent magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain looking for hypoxic ischaemic injury or cortical malformation
options.rationale: MRI is important but the immediate need is to exclude treatable metabolic causes with EEG-supported diagnosis before empirical anticonvulsants; MRI can follow. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures)

options.text: Administer a 100 mg intravenous pyridoxine trial with concurrent continuous electroencephalography monitoring
options.rationale: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy presents in the neonate with normal glucose, electrolytes and ammonia, bland CSF and normal imaging; an EEG-monitored IV pyridoxine trial is diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures)

options.text: Request very-long-chain fatty acids and organic acids on plasma to screen for peroxisomal disorders as the priority test
options.rationale: These tests can be sent but will not return within a clinically useful timeframe; a pyridoxine trial is faster and both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures)

options.text: Administer intravenous 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kilogram bolus followed by 6 mg per kilogram per minute infusion for hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Her glucose is 3.6 mmol/L which is within the term neonatal range beyond 24 hours; dextrose bolus is not the pertinent intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Seizures)

explanation.summary: Neonatal seizures require a stepwise workup for treatable causes before empirical anticonvulsants. First-line correctable causes include hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and inborn errors of metabolism with high ammonia. When glucose, electrolytes, ammonia, CSF and imaging are unremarkable but seizures continue, pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (autosomal recessive antiquitin gene mutation) should be considered. An EEG-monitored pyridoxine trial of 100 mg IV is both diagnostic and therapeutic; seizure and EEG normalisation within minutes establishes the diagnosis and warrants lifelong maintenance therapy. Phenobarbitone remains first-line empirical anticonvulsant when seizures continue and no treatable metabolic cause is identified.
key_points: Correct hypoglycaemia, sodium, calcium, magnesium and treat ammonia first.
Pyridoxine trial for seizures with normal metabolic workup and imaging.
EEG monitoring during the trial confirms electroclinical response.
Phenobarbitone is first-line anticonvulsant otherwise.
explanation.pearls: For a neonate with ongoing seizures and normal glucose, electrolytes, ammonia and imaging, a 100 mg IV pyridoxine trial under EEG monitoring is both diagnostic and therapeutic for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy.
